name: Cleaning business
blurb: Clean homes or offices for a fee per visit, ideally on a weekly or fortnightly schedule
title: How to Start a Cleaning Business: Costs, Pricing and Risks
description: How a house or office cleaning business makes money, what you need to start, who it suits, the real risks and how to test demand with a few paid jobs first.
h1: How to start a cleaning business
answer: A cleaning business is paid to clean homes, offices or rental properties, usually per visit or per hour, and the best clients book on a repeating schedule. Startup costs are low because supplies and a few tools are enough to begin. The catch is that the work is physical, competition is wide, and your income is capped by the hours you or your staff can clean.

sections.h: How a cleaning business makes money
body: You charge per hour, per visit or a flat price per job (for example a move-out clean or an end-of-tenancy clean). Recurring clients on a weekly or fortnightly schedule are the core: they fill your calendar without fresh marketing every week.

Margin goes to travel time between jobs, supplies, insurance, cancellations and, once you hire, wages and payroll costs. Office and commercial contracts pay steadily but are often won on price and can be cancelled when the client changes supplier.

ul: Cleaning supplies and basic equipment: a good vacuum, microfibre cloths, mops and products you can use safely on different surfaces.
Transport that can carry your kit between jobs.
Insurance: public or general liability covers damage to a client's property; ask whether you also need bonding or cover for keys and breakages.
Local paperwork: rules differ by country and city. In many places you register as self-employed or form a business and may need a local business licence; check with your local authority.
A simple booking and invoicing system, plus a written checklist for each type of clean so quality stays the same.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: People who enjoy visible, practical results
Anyone with back, joint or allergy problems
Someone who wants to start with little money
People who want income that grows without adding hours
Organised people who keep promises and keys safe
Anyone uncomfortable working alone in strangers' homes

ul: Underpricing: many new cleaners quote low to win work and then cannot afford to raise prices or hire help. Include travel time and supplies in every quote.
Damage and accusations: a broken item or a missing valuable can cost far more than the job. Insurance, a clear breakage policy and checklists protect you.
Cancellations and no-shows: agree a cancellation policy in writing before the first visit.
Client concentration: one large office contract can be most of your income until it is suddenly not.
Hiring brings employment rules, training and quality control; a bad cleaner under your name can lose clients quickly.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: Search maps and local listings for cleaners in your area and note what they offer.
Clean three homes for friends or neighbours at a real price and time each job honestly.
Ask each of them whether they would book again and what they would pay for a regular slot.
Post one clear offer in a local community group and count the genuine enquiries in two weeks.
Work out your hourly earnings after travel and supplies; if it is below what you would accept from a job, adjust the offer or stop.
Register the business, get liability insurance and check any local licence you need.
Pick one niche to start: regular home cleans, move-out cleans or small offices.
Write a checklist and a price list, including a minimum charge and a cancellation policy.
Ask every happy client for a review and a referral.
Group clients by area so travel time does not eat your day.
Only think about hiring once your own calendar is consistently full.

faq.q: How much should I charge for house cleaning?
faq.a: Prices vary widely by city, so check what local cleaners charge and work back from the hourly income you need after travel, supplies and tax. Many cleaners quote a flat price per home once they know how long it takes, with a higher first-visit price for a deep clean.

faq.q: Do I need insurance to start a cleaning business?
faq.a: It is strongly advisable and many clients, especially offices and letting agents, will ask for proof of liability insurance. Requirements differ by country, so check what applies where you work.

faq.q: Is residential or commercial cleaning better to start with?
faq.a: Home cleaning is easier to start because individual clients book quickly through referrals. Commercial work can be steadier but often involves evening hours, tenders and price pressure, and losing one contract hurts more.
